title: The dissents
primary_topics: Cybercrime Prevention Law dissents doctrinal column March 16, 2014 -- second installment of two-part cybercrime arc (A423 Mar 9 → A422 Mar 16)
SC decision (Jesus Disini v. SOJ, Feb 18, 2014) upheld constitutionality of libel both printed and online; back-reference to A423 explainer
Sec. 6 CPL: online libel penalized 'one degree higher' than RPC -- from 6 months-and-1-day-to-4-years-2-months → 6 years-and-1-day-to-10-years imprisonment

Sereno dissent on Sec. 6 'invidious chilling effect': accessory penalty of 'temporary absolute perpetual disqualification' (deprivation of public office + right to vote/be voted + retirement pay/pension); neutralizes probation-law benefits (probation for crimes ≤6 years); 10x prescription period (1 year → 10 years for online libel)

Carpio dissent: declare Art. 354 RPC unconstitutional as applied to public officers and public figures -- presumes existence of malice in every defamatory imputation, ipso facto punishable 'even if it be true, if no good intention and justifiable motive for making it is shown'

Carpio framework: SC has consistently held -- following American jurisprudence -- that criticism of public officials is protected by constitutional right to free expression and cannot be penalized 'even if such criticism is defamatory and false'; only way to overturn is to prove 'actual malice' (knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard)

Borjal v. Court of Appeals (Jan 14, 1999) extension of actual-malice rule to public figures -- 'person who, by his accomplishments, fame, mode of living, or by adopting a profession or calling gives the public a legitimate interest in his doings, his affairs and his character... anyone who has arrived at a position where the public attention is focused upon him as a person'

Majority upheld actual-malice rule but found no need to void Art. 354 because existing jurisprudence already limits its scope; CJP thinks it better to declare Art. 354 unconstitutional 'as far as it applies to public officials and public figures' to stress Constitution's supremacy and Court's devotion to free speech

Leonen dissent: libel completely unconstitutional -- 'continued criminalization especially in platforms using the internet unqualifiedly produces a chilling effect that stifles our fundamental guarantees of free expression... Criminalizing libel contradicts our notions of a genuinely democratic society'; Leonen-historical-frame: libel used by Spanish + American colonizers to suppress independence-supportive speech; after independence, now used by 'powerful and influential to silence their critics'; Dean Raul Pangalangan study -- libel cases pursued mainly by public figures, private-person cases 'settled before the prosecutor'; civil remedy via injunction + damages

CJP's three-tier closing endorsement: (1) libel should be decriminalized (Leonen) (2) at very least, Art. 354 should be declared unconstitutional (Carpio) (3) higher penalty for online libel should be declared unconstitutional (Sereno); final note on Inquirer online comments -- 'inevitably the public can discern truth from propaganda, objectivity from prejudice, and credibility from implausibility... liars and charlatans expose themselves and lose respect... vindication for those who believe in the liberating power of free speech'
sub_topics: SC decision (Jesus Disini v. SOJ, Feb 18, 2014) on Cybercrime Prevention Law (CPL) upheld constitutionality of libel (both printed and online), as CJP explained last Sunday (A423)
CJP will now discuss portions of dissents that he finds reasonable
To be sure, CPL has several provisions on libel
Sec. 6 of law states online libel shall be penalized 'one degree higher than that provided for by the Revised Penal Code'
Simply stated, this legalese means penalty is increased from range of 'six months and one day to four years and two months' imprisonment to range of 'six years and one day to 10 years' imprisonment
Majority upheld this section on ground that severity of penalties is law-making, not judicial, prerogative
CJ Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno dissented, arguing more severe penalty has 'invidious chilling effect'
Aside from being lengthened to 10 years, carries accessory penalty of 'temporary absolute perpetual disqualification'
Means deprivation of (1) any public office offender may hold (2) right to vote and be voted to public office (3) retirement pay and pension
Higher penalty also 'neutralizes the full benefits of the law on probation'
Under probation law, those convicted of crimes penalized by not more than six years imprisonment, and who renounce right to appeal, may avoid incarceration and 'undergo rehabilitation outside prison'
Since CPL increased penalty to maximum of 10 years, this benefit denied to cyberlibel offenders
Higher penalty also lengthens prescription period of crime from one year to 10 years
In lay terms: printed libel charge can be filed within one year only from commission, online libel complaint can be instituted within 10 years
Thus, threat of prosecution for online libel lingers 10 times longer
Justice Antonio T. Carpio voted 'to declare unconstitutional Article 354 of the RPC as far as it applies to public officers and public figures'
This article presumes existence of malice in every defamatory imputation
Thus making it ipso facto punishable, 'even if it be true, if no good intention and justifiable motive for making it is shown'
However, SC has consistently held -- following American jurisprudence -- that criticism of public officials is protected by constitutional right to free expression
And cannot be penalized 'even if such criticism is defamatory and false'
Only way to overturn this protection is to prove defamatory statement was made with 'actual malice'
I.e., with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not
Actual malice rule was later extended to public figures

According to Borjal v. Court of Appeals (Jan 14, 1999), public figure is 'a person who, by his accomplishments, fame, mode of living, or by adopting a profession or calling gives the public a legitimate interest in his doings, his affairs and his character'
'In short, anyone who has arrived at a position where the public attention is focused upon him as a person' due to celebrity or notoriety
Significantly, majority upheld actual malice rule but found no need to void Art. 354 because existing jurisprudence already limits its scope
CJP thinks, however, it is better to declare it unconstitutional 'as far as it applies to public officials and public figures' to stress Constitution's supremacy and Court's devotion to free speech
Justice Marvic Mario Victor F. Leonen went further by holding that libel is completely unconstitutional
He stressed that 'its continued criminalization especially in platforms using the [I]nternet unqualifiedly produces a chilling effect that stifles our fundamental guarantees of free expression'
'Criminalizing libel contradicts our notions of a genuinely democratic society'
Historically, libel was used by our colonizers, Spaniards and Americans, to suppress speech critical of foreign rule and supportive of independence
After independence was attained, criminal libel, he added, is now used by 'the powerful and influential to silence their critics'
Citing study by Dean Raul Pangalangan that 'libel cases are pursued to their conclusion mainly by public figures... those filed by private persons are settled before the prosecutor'
'Legal remedy of the maligned is civil in nature... facts that will constitute the cause of action will be narrowly tailored to address the perceived wrong'
Relief is injunction and damages
In sum, CJP believes:
(1) libel should be decriminalized as held by J Leonen, or
(2) at very least, Art. 354 of RPC should be declared unconstitutional as opined by J Carpio, and
(3) higher penalty for online libel should be declared unconstitutional, as detailed by CJ Sereno
Final note: Inquirer articles are posted online and subjected to comments and reactions, whether fair and objective or malicious and skewed
These vibrant interactions show that inevitably the public can discern truth from propaganda, objectivity from prejudice, and credibility from implausibility
Invariably, liars and charlatans expose themselves and lose respect
That should be enough vindication for those who believe in the liberating power of free speech

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban writes the second installment of his two-part cybercrime arc, discussing the dissents he finds reasonable. The SC decision (Jesus Disini v. SOJ, Feb 18, 2014) on the Cybercrime Prevention Law (CPL) upheld the constitutionality of libel (both printed and online), as CJ explained last Sunday (A423); CJ will now discuss portions of the dissents that he finds reasonable. Sereno dissent: to be sure, the CPL has several provisions on libel. Sec. 6 of the law states that online libel shall be penalized 'one degree higher than that provided for by the RPC' -- simply stated, this legalese means the penalty is increased from a range of '6 months and 1 day to 4 years and 2 months' imprisonment to a range of '6 years and 1 day to 10 years' imprisonment. The majority upheld this section on the ground that the severity of penalties is a law-making, not judicial, prerogative. CJ Maria Lourdes P.A. Sereno dissented, arguing that the more severe penalty has an 'invidious chilling effect' because, aside from being lengthened to 10 years, it carries the accessory penalty of 'temporary absolute perpetual disqualification' -- deprivation of (1) any public office the offender may hold, (2) the right to vote and be voted to public office, and (3) retirement pay and pension. The higher penalty also 'neutralizes the full benefits of the law on probation' -- under this law, those convicted of crimes penalized by not more than 6 years imprisonment, who renounce their right to appeal, may avoid incarceration and 'undergo rehabilitation outside prison'; since the CPL increased the penalty to a maximum of 10 years, this benefit is denied to cyberlibel offenders. Also, the higher penalty lengthens the prescription period of the crime from 1 year to 10 years -- in lay terms, while a printed libel charge can be filed within 1 year only from its commission, an online libel complaint can be instituted within 10 years; thus, the threat of prosecution for online libel lingers 10 times longer. Carpio dissent: Justice Antonio T. Carpio voted 'to declare unconstitutional Article 354 of the RPC as far as it applies to public officers and public figures' -- this article presumes the existence of malice in every defamatory imputation, thus making it ipso facto punishable, 'even if it be true, if no good intention and justifiable motive for making it is shown.' However, the SC has consistently held -- following American jurisprudence -- that criticism of public officials is protected by the constitutional right to free expression and cannot be penalized 'even if such criticism is defamatory and false.' The only way to overturn this protection is to prove that the defamatory statement was made with 'actual malice, that is, with knowledge that it was false or with a reckless disregard of whether it was false or not.' The actual malice rule was later extended to public figures -- according to Borjal v. CA (Jan 14, 1999), a public figure is 'a person who, by his accomplishments, fame, mode of living, or by adopting a profession or calling gives the public a legitimate interest in his doings, his affairs and his character... in short, anyone who has arrived at a position where the public attention is focused upon him as a person' due to his or her celebrity or notoriety. Significantly, the majority upheld the actual malice rule but found no need to void Art. 354 because existing jurisprudence already limits its scope -- CJ thinks, however, that it is better to declare it unconstitutional 'as far as it applies to public officials and public figures' to stress the Constitution's supremacy and the Court's devotion to free speech. Leonen dissent: Justice Marvic Mario Victor F. Leonen went further by holding that libel is completely unconstitutional; he stressed that 'its continued criminalization especially in platforms using the [I]nternet unqualifiedly produces a chilling effect that stifles our fundamental guarantees of free expression... Criminalizing libel contradicts our notions of a genuinely democratic society.' Historically, libel was used by our colonizers, the Spaniards and the Americans, to suppress speech critical of foreign rule and supportive of independence; after independence was attained, criminal libel is now used by 'the powerful and influential to silence their critics,' citing a study made by Dean Raul Pangalangan that 'libel cases are pursued to their conclusion mainly by public figures... [those filed] by private persons are settled before the prosecutor.' The 'legal remedy [of the maligned] is civil in nature... [where] the facts that will constitute the cause of action will be narrowly tailored to address the perceived wrong' -- the relief is injunction and damages. In sum, CJ believes (1) libel should be decriminalized as held by J. Leonen; or (2) at the very least, Art. 354 of the RPC should be declared unconstitutional as opined by J. Carpio; and (3) the higher penalty for online libel should be declared unconstitutional, as detailed by CJ Sereno. A final note: Inquirer articles are posted online and subjected to comments and reactions, whether fair and objective or malicious and skewed -- these vibrant interactions show that inevitably the public can discern truth from propaganda, objectivity from prejudice, and credibility from implausibility; invariably, liars and charlatans expose themselves and lose respect; that should be enough vindication for those who believe in the liberating power of free speech.
